facts.text: Tamaqua was originally to be named Tuscarora, but the name Tamaqua was chosen after realizing another Tuscarora existed nearby.
The 55‑block Tamaqua Historic District, including the Anthracite Bank Building and George Ormrod House, is on the National Register of Historic Places.
The town’s Victorian‑era train station, built in 1874, still stands and houses the Tamaqua Historical Society Museum.
Tamaqua’s roots trace back to 1799 when settlers Burkhardt Moser, Jacob Moser, and John Kershner built a sawmill at the Little Schuylkill River and Panther Creek confluence.
In the 1840s and 1850s, Irish, Welsh, and German immigrants settled Tamaqua, followed by large waves of Italians, Lithuanians, Russians, Ukrainians, Slovaks, and Poles in the 1890s.
The active Reading, Blue Mountain & Northern Railroad still crosses the borough north‑south west of Five Points, a junction of PA Routes 209, 309, and Mauch Chunk Street.
